analysis.one_liner: Exempts oil, gas, coal, and mining permits on federal lands from environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would skip environmental review for oil, gas, coal, and hardrock mining on federal lands, has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since January 2025 with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make oil, gas, and coal leases and permits for mining critical minerals on federal land exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the law that requires federal agencies to study and disclose the environmental impacts of major projects before approving them [S2][S3]. If it passed, companies leasing federal land for drilling, mining, or pipelines would no longer have to prepare environmental impact statements or environmental assessments for those decisions, and the public would lose the review and comment process that NEPA provides [S2]. The bill was introduced by Representative Harriet Hageman and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where no further action has been taken [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies leasing federal land and hardrock mining companies claiming critical minerals would benefit most: they could obtain and renew federal leases and permits without environmental impact studies, public comment periods, or the litigation risk that NEPA review creates. That can mean faster approvals and lower compliance costs for extraction projects [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: It removes NEPA review — the requirement to study and disclose environmental impacts before a decision — from federal leases, easements, and rights-of-way for oil, gas, and coal exploration, development, and production under the Mineral Leasing Act.
It removes NEPA review from federal permits for exploring and extracting critical minerals on public land open to mining under the Mining Law of 1872.
For companies, skipping NEPA review means avoiding multi-year studies, public comment processes, and a common basis for lawsuits that delay or block extraction projects.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near federal lands opened to drilling or mining, and the public generally, would bear the cost: no agency study of air, water, wildlife, or community impacts before approval, and no public comment window to raise concerns. Taxpayers and nearby residents also bear cleanup, health, and water-contamination risks that review exists to identify in advance [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near drilling and mining sites

drawbacks.text: Without NEPA review, federal agencies would approve drilling and mining on public land with no required analysis of impacts on air, water, wildlife, and nearby communities, and no public comment period for affected residents — the review process would be eliminated, not reformed.
The bill is written broadly: it covers renewals of existing leases and permits as well as new ones, so even previously reviewed operations could be extended without any updated environmental study.

A supporter would argue NEPA reviews can take years and hold up energy production and critical-mineral supply chains; the bill addresses that delay by removing the review entirely rather than shortening or streamlining it, leaving no substitute analysis of project risks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The speed gained by industry is real, but it comes entirely from deleting environmental analysis and public participation rather than streamlining them. The public gives up the only required look at what drilling and mining on federal land would do to water, air, and nearby communities, with no replacement safeguard. The scale of the benefit is hard to judge because the bill has no supporting analysis and no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and has sat there without cosponsors, a hearing, or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Harriet Hageman introduced the bill on January 23, 2025.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
No cosponsors have joined, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained much from the bill's inaction except that communities near federal drilling and mining sites have kept the existing environmental review requirement it would remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities keeping environmental review, so far

for.name: Rep. Harriet Hageman
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt federal energy and mineral actions on federal lands from NEPA review.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in over a year.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote, so there is no record of where the parties stand beyond the sponsor's own action.

industries.note: The bill lets them obtain and renew federal leases without environmental impact studies, public comment, or the litigation exposure NEPA creates, saving years and compliance costs. The saving comes directly from skipping the analysis of drilling's effects on nearby communities and public resources.

Permits to explore and extract critical minerals on open public land would no longer require any environmental review under this bill. The Mining Law of 1872 already charges no royalties for hardrock minerals on public land, so the added benefit to miners is a pure cost saving borne by the public.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a year after referral, the bill is very likely to sit in the Natural Resources Committee until this Congress ends, which is the usual fate of single-sponsor bills without leadership backing. It could only move if the committee chair or House leadership decides to prioritize it.
